text:
emily: Customer reports Redwood Private control plane connections failing after they pushed an egress firewall update this morning. Symptoms: internal CNF apps started getting: "tls: handshake failure" and control plane logs show TLS alert 40. They say it worked before the firewall change.

javier: quick ask — can we get the exact error from the customer app and a tcpdump showing the ClientHello? often this is SNI or client cert chain related.

customer (via emily): attaching the app log snippet they sent: 
`2026-03-10T09:12:14Z error: dial tcp 10.11.12.13:443: tls: handshake error: remote error: tls: handshake failure`

lina: also ask them to run: `openssl s_client -connect controlplane.example.com:443 -servername controlplane.example.com -cert client.pem -key client.key -alpn h2 -tls1_2` and paste output. if SNI gets rewritten you'll see a different ServerName in the handshake response.

arjun: note that many NGFWs rewrite CNAMEs or terminate TLS for inspection which breaks mTLS — the firewall must NOT terminate or rewrite SNI for mTLS control-plane flows.

javier: customer ran openssl and pasted the ClientHello/server side debug snippet: 
```
CONNECTED(00000003)
---
New, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
---
Server certificate:
subject=/CN=controlplane.internal.corp
---
>>> TLS 1.3 Handshake, ClientHello
    extensions: server_name: controlplane.cust-public.example.com
```
The server cert CN is controlplane.internal.corp but ClientHello SNI was controlplane.cust-public.example.com -> looks like a CNAME flatten/translation.

support-bot: @support created #INC-4321 and attached the tcpdump.

arjun: that mismatch alone wouldn't cause a handshake failure for mTLS unless the f/w is doing TLS inspection and presenting its own cert or stripping the client cert. Two common patterns: (1) firewall is doing SSL forward proxy and presenting its own cert (breaks mTLS), (2) SNI rewriting to a different name that our control plane doesn't accept for client cert verification.

lina: repro steps for customer to check locally (one-liners):
`dig +short controlplane.example.com`
`dig +short @8.8.8.8 controlplane.example.com CNAME`
`openssl s_client -connect <ip>:443 -servername <ip-or-name> -status -showcerts`
Also tcpdump: `sudo tcpdump -n -s 0 -w /tmp/cp.pcap host controlplane.example.com and port 443`

javier: I asked them to run `tcpdump -A -s 0 'tcp port 443 and host 10.11.12.13' | sed -n '1,200p'` and the dump shows a TLS ClientHello where the SNI header is being rewritten to `corp-proxy.local` by the egress device. That's a smoking gun for TLS inspection.

customer (via emily): their firewall team confirmed they added an HTTPS inspection policy that intercepts external TLS and does a re-sign with their internal CA. They said they thought control plane traffic was regular HTTPS.

arjun: solution path: for mTLS to work we need end-to-end TLS passthrough (no MITM). Ask customer firewall to create an allowlist/passthrough rule for control plane FQDNs or the explicit public IP ranges used by Redwood Private control plane. Provide list of IP ranges or ASN (we also gave them our published control plane IP set). Also ensure ALPN (h2) is preserved and TLS 1.2/1.3 not downgraded.

lina: temporary workaround if they cannot change the firewall: use a dedicated egress NAT pool that bypasses inspection for the service CIDR, or route control plane traffic through a bastion that has no TLS inspection. Not ideal but buys time.

javier: also check that the customer's client cert chain includes the intermediate certs; some proxies accept client cert but drop intermediates and server will reject. Ask for `openssl s_client -connect ... -showcerts` output to confirm.

emily: suggested message to customer firewall team I gave them:
```
Please exempt the following hostnames/IPs from TLS inspection and SNI rewrite for mTLS traffic to Redwood Private control plane. TLS must be passthrough so the client certificate is presented end-to-end. Keep ALPN and TLS1.3 intact.
- controlplane.cust-public.example.com
- <list of redwood control plane IPs we provided>
If exemption is not possible, route control-plane API traffic via a non-inspected egress or provide a dedicated NAT IP pool.
```

oncall-bot: paging network-eng oncall for verification of control plane IPs.

javier: customer made the firewall change to allow passthrough for the control plane IPs and confirmed after 5 minutes that the handshake succeeded. They reported app logs now show successful dial and the control plane accepted their client cert.

emily: customer confirmed remediation: "we removed TLS inspection for controlplane addresses and verified client cert chain; things are green now." :white_check_mark:

lina: I'll add a KB note recommending customers configure TLS passthrough for Redwood Private mTLS and provide the exact IP lists and SNI patterns to support.

emily: closing loop with customer and will mark the support case resolved after they verify for 24 hours. Thanks all.
